Fraser's shrew (Crocidura poensis) is a small-bodied eulipotyphlan from West African forests about which relatively little physiological data have been published, though comparative estimates derived from the better-studied Crocidura russula provide a useful framework. Neonates of this species weigh approximately 0.95 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.95 grams] at birth, a value consistent with the altricial condition typical of many crocidurine shrews. The neonatal pups are born hairless and fully dependent on maternal care, with a wet weight at birth that places them among the smaller offspring within the genus. This modest initial mass reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a high metabolic demand even at this early developmental stage, as the mothers must allocate substantial resources to lactation almost immediately after parturition. The wet weight at weaning has been reported at 7.8 grams [Wwx = 7.8 grams], representing a roughly eightfold increase from the newborn mass that occurs over a relatively brief nursing interval. This growth trajectory underscores the intense parental investment required during the pre-weaning period, a pattern shared with other small insectivorous mammals that face high mass-specific metabolic costs.

Under captive conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Crocidura poensis is inferred to be 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 pups per litter], with females capable of producing three and a half litters per year [F_R_i = three and a half litters per year]. This reproductive schedule, extrapolated from congeneric data, suggests a high annual fecundity that likely offsets substantial juvenile mortality in the wild. The reproductive cycle is rapid, reflecting a life-history strategy adapted to unpredictable resource availability in humid tropical environments. The gestation period at this same thermal regime lasts 29 days [tg = 29 days], a relatively short interval that allows females to compress multiple breeding events within a single season at a temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. The combination of moderate litter size and frequent reproductive bouts positions this species as a typical r-selected small mammal, though the exact values should be confirmed through direct field observation of West African populations rather than relying solely on comparative models.

The duration of maternal investment after parturition is precisely constrained by the weaning period, with offspring achieving nutritional independence at 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth] under a maintained temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This relatively short lactation phase is characteristic of small shrews that must wean their young quickly to allow the mother to initiate subsequent pregnancies. The time since birth at weaning represents a critical developmental boundary, after which juveniles must begin foraging independently despite their still-limited body size. Following weaning, the young undergo a period of rapid somatic growth before reaching maturity. The maximum adult body mass for Crocidura poensis is 17.3 grams [Wwi = 17.3 grams], a value that falls within the typical range for forest-dwelling shrews of this genus but is notably lower than the mass attained by some larger African congeners. This ultimate wet weight is achieved shortly after the onset of independent feeding, with individuals then maintaining this mass throughout their reproductive lives.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at 75 days after birth [tp = 75 days after birth] under the same stable thermal conditions of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], marking the transition from the juvenile stage to a reproductively viable adult capable of breeding. The timing of puberty reflects the relatively fast pace of life history in small crocidurines, where early reproduction is favored by high extrinsic mortality rates. The age at first reproduction likely coincides closely with the attainment of sexual maturity, as females typically breed during their first opportunity. Estimated from Crocidura russula under these thermoneutral conditions, the maximum lifespan is approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days], which equates to roughly four years of life at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This longevity is moderate for a mammal of its size, though many individuals in natural populations likely succumb to predation or environmental stressors well before reaching this maximum potential age. Senescence in captivity is typically preceded by a gradual decline in body condition and reproductive output.

Basal metabolic rate measurements for Crocidura poensis, as predicted from allometric equations and adjusted for body mass, indicate a maximum oxygen consumption of 31.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This resting metabolic rate is characteristic of insectivorous small mammals with high mass-specific energy demands, reflecting the energetic cost of maintaining homeothermy at a small body size. The elevated metabolic rate has profound implications for the species' foraging ecology, requiring individuals to consume prey items frequently throughout the day to avoid rapid depletion of energy stores. In comparative terms, this value aligns closely with predictions for a 17.3 gram [Wwi = 17.3 gram] insectivore, reinforcing the tight coupling between body mass and metabolic expenditure in this genus. The consistency of these estimates with Crocidura russula data suggests that, despite geographic separation, the two species share remarkably similar energetic and life-history profiles when measured under equivalent thermal conditions. Future field studies targeting West African populations would be valuable to validate these inferred parameters directly.
